title: Indianapolis

jokes.text: Ron's suggestion that Leslie just speak alone at the commendation ceremony
jokes.setup: Leslie is excitedly working out every permutation of who should speak first at the ceremony — 'me and then you,' 'you and then me,' 'me, you, me'
jokes.punchline: Ron, utterly indifferent, cuts through all of it: 'How about just you?'
jokes.explanation: A tight cold open joke. The setup perfectly captures Leslie's neurotic enthusiasm while Ron's one-line dismissal is exactly in his character. The structure is clean — escalating absurdity from Leslie followed by maximum economy from Ron. Character integration is very high: only Ron could deliver this with this level of weaponized boredom.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could do it alphabetically by first name, or by last name, or by department, or by tenure, or we could do a rotating system where each person speaks for exactly four minutes and thirty seconds...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head about photographing every steak he's ever eaten at Charles Mulligan's
jokes.setup: Ron says Indianapolis is home to the best steakhouse in the state and that he has been there many times
jokes.punchline: He has taken a photograph of every steak he has ever eaten there — framed as a completely reasonable, almost sentimental practice
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The concept of photographing steaks like cherished memories of loved ones is absurd but completely consistent with Ron's established reverence for meat. The deadpan delivery and the framing as something entirely normal elevates it. Character integration is near-perfect — this is *only* Ron Swanson.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't care about awards. My only motivation is steak. Everything else is just noise.

jokes.text: Ron narrating steak photos like a war veteran's photo album — date, cut, sauce, and then 'The lady next to me: A bitch.'
jokes.setup: Ron recites steak details in the precise, reverent cadence of someone describing important historical documents — June 2004, porterhouse, medium rare, béarnaise sauce; January 2000, 'The Enforcer'; February '96, rib-eye, Lagavulin 16
jokes.punchline: 'The lady next to me: A bitch. Specifically, my ex-wife Tammy.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is immaculate — three steak entries delivered in an escalating, ritualistic format, lulling the audience into the pattern, then smashing it with the flat, matter-of-fact description of an ex-wife as 'a bitch.' The word 'specifically' adds a layer of bureaucratic precision that makes it funnier. Only Ron Swanson would include his ex-wife's presence as a neutral data point in steak records, and only Ron would describe her with such economy. Hugely quotable. Near the 9.5 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a document here that details every steak I've eaten in the last 20 years. Cut, weight, temperature, sauce selection, establishment, date, time of day, and my emotional state before consumption.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm currently on my 847th steak. I have a five-year projection that accounts for seasonal availability and my declining digestive capabilities.

jokes.text: 'Oh, look at me. I'm just a kid.' — Ron looking at his first steak photo with nostalgic wonder
jokes.setup: Ron has been treating steak photos with the gravity of a life well-lived; the last photo shown is his very first visit
jokes.punchline: He looks at young himself with the same wistful nostalgia a person uses looking at childhood photos, but it's about steak
jokes.explanation: A perfect button to the steak photo sequence. The callback deepens the joke: Ron treats his meat-eating history with genuine sentimentality. 'Just a kid' is the punchline because of how earnestly Ron believes this is a legitimate nostalgic milestone. Short, character-perfect, earns its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been cataloguing these steak photos by marbling quality, cooking temperature, and the bitch who took half my stuff in the divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy Two.

jokes.text: Dennis Feinstein's new cologne is called 'Allergic — For Men'
jokes.setup: Tom announces there's a launch party at the Snakehole Lounge for a new fragrance
jokes.punchline: The fragrance is called 'Allergic — For Men'
jokes.explanation: Strong absurdist comedy name-joke. 'Allergic' is a brilliantly terrible cologne name because it implies the exact opposite of sensory pleasure. The 'For Men' suffix is a deadpan corporate touch that makes it funnier. Good economy, good originality.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? This old thing? I just threw it on.

jokes.text: Dennis Feinstein's ether-based perfume 'Blackout' was named one of Maxim's top 100 ways to trick someone into sex
jokes.setup: Tom is building up Dennis Feinstein's credentials as a microbrewed perfume mogul
jokes.punchline: His flagship product was designed and celebrated as a tool for sexual assault, framed matter-of-factly as a business credential
jokes.explanation: Dark and absurdist in the Parks & Rec tradition of making Pawnee itself a villain. Framing a deeply criminal product as a legitimate business achievement delivered in Tom's credulous hype-man voice is sharply written. The joke ages uncomfortably given later cultural conversations, which is worth noting, but in pure craft terms the satirical absurdity is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dennis Feinstein has accomplished so much. He's built an empire, created thousands of jobs, and revolutionized the candy industry.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Plus, he's only been indicted three times.

jokes.text: 'Oh, no, no, way too late. I will be deep into my bath by then.'
jokes.setup: The club event starts at 9pm; everyone else treats this as normal
jokes.punchline: Ron rejects it not because he dislikes clubs, but because 9pm is bath time — stated with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Ron's extreme domesticity (bath by 9pm) contrasted with the sleazy club setting, and his utter lack of embarrassment about it. 'Deep into my bath' is a particularly good phrase — the word 'deep' suggesting total commitment to the bath. Very Ron-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You know what I hate about Facebook? It's all these pointless status updates from people you haven't talked to in ten years. Like, 'Just made a sandwich.' Great. Thanks for sharing that with 847 of your closest friends.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head about Facebook friends — 'Hey, Doug from Bloomington is thinking about buying a shirt. I mean, come on, Doug, who cares?'
jokes.setup: Ben explains that because he moves around so much, the friends he makes feel superficial — like Facebook friends
jokes.punchline: He illustrates with a specific, perfectly mundane Facebook status update and his exasperated response to it
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Doug from Bloomington' and 'thinking about buying a shirt' is what elevates this above a generic social media observation. The follow-up 'who cares?' captures Ben's deadpan weariness perfectly. Good structure — the confessional format gives the joke space to breathe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I need you to help Ben be more social. He's too stiff, too formal.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'd love to help, but I'm only 5'4". How am I supposed to reach him?

jokes.text: 'Come on, Tom, take him under your tiny little wing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking Tom to befriend Ben and take him to the party
jokes.punchline: She insults Tom's physical stature mid-request, apparently without realizing or caring
jokes.explanation: A well-placed throwaway insult that works because Leslie delivers it with complete sincerity. The 'tiny little' is a nice bit of Leslie obliviousness — she means it as a metaphor but it lands as a physical dig. Solid mid-range joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, our new album is called 'Love's Tender Embrace: A Journey Through the Moonlit Gardens of My Heart Where Every Flower Represents a Different Aspect of Your Beauty and Also There's a Song About Your Eyes, Specifically the Left One'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's a double album.

jokes.text: Tom's pitch for his cologne 'Tommy Fresh' — 'I spray him and say, Uh-oh. Looks like you just nailed your future.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Tom to take Ben out; Tom says tonight is business — he's pitching his own cologne to Dennis Feinstein
jokes.punchline: His planned pitch line is 'Uh-oh. Looks like you just nailed your future' — delivered with complete confidence in its brilliance
jokes.explanation: The joke is Tom's total conviction in a pitch line that is completely meaningless. 'Nailed your future' sounds like cologne copy but means nothing. Tom's confidence is the joke. Character integration is high — Tom's delusion about his own brilliance is a core trait.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so when you're dating someone, you have to, like, pay for things? For both of you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I thought that was just a thing rich people did.

jokes.text: April's band's album is called 'April Ludgate Is the Best Ever, Volume One'
jokes.setup: Andy casually mentions his band is working on a new album and April asks what it's called
jokes.punchline: The album is named after April — maximum sycophancy delivered as if it's a normal band decision
jokes.explanation: 'Volume One' is the key detail that makes this joke land — it implies there will be more, and Andy has no doubt about this. It's pure Andy Dwyer: earnest, over-the-top romantic, completely unselfconscious. April's 'Shut up' is the perfect reaction: half-dismissal, half-pleased. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want to get April a gift that says 'I love you' but also 'I respect your personal space.' So I'm thinking a high-end vibrator.

jokes.text: April's 'Shut up.' reaction to the album name
jokes.setup: Andy reveals the album is called 'April Ludgate Is the Best Ever, Volume One'
jokes.punchline: April's flat, dismissive 'Shut up' — which in context reads as embarrassed pleasure
jokes.explanation: Economy is perfect — one word does all the work. April's 'Shut up' is calibrated exactly to her character: she would never say 'aw, that's sweet.' The joke is in what the dismissal reveals.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm in a relationship. It's fine. He's fine. Everything's fine. I don't really like talking about my feelings because then I have to have feelings about my feelings, and I don't have time for that.

jokes.text: Andy and April's date night options: watch TV at Burly's, watch TV at April's, or watch TV at Best Buy
jokes.setup: Andy asks April what she wants to do tonight
jokes.punchline: All three options are watching TV — just in different locations, with Best Buy being a completely sincere suggestion
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates through mundanity to the absurd Best Buy suggestion. Andy doesn't realize he's offered three identical options. The third option — a retail store — as a legitimate date venue is a good character beat for broke, unsophisticated Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've always had a knack for detective work. In high school, they called me 'Sherlock'.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because of your deductive skills?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, because I had really big teeth and a long face.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head about what he wants to give April — escalating from flowers to 'different kinds of lubes that warm up when you rub 'em on stuff'
jokes.setup: Andy explains he wants to treat April like a queen, listing gifts
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from romantic (flowers, chocolates) to opulent (diamonds, rubies, emeralds) to bizarre ('them treasure chests full of scarves') to explicit ('different kinds of lubes that warm up when you rub 'em on stuff') — all delivered with equal earnestness
jokes.explanation: Masterfully structured escalation. The list starts conventionally romantic, moves through aspirational (jewels), takes a strange left turn (treasure chests of scarves — why scarves specifically?), and lands on an explicit item stated with the same earnest sincerity as 'flowers.' The specificity of 'warm up when you rub 'em on stuff' as a selling feature shows Andy's complete lack of filter. The scarves detail is inspired absurdism. High originality, exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm not going to some pathetically sad motel. I'm going to the Motel 6. They leave the light on for you.

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'I don't know. I guess we're dating. It's new. Whatever. I don't like labels.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April just agreed to go out together
jokes.punchline: April, in confessional, tries to project cool indifference about what is clearly a relationship she cares about
jokes.explanation: Classic April Ludgate deflection. The joke is the gap between her projected indifference and the obvious warmth of the situation. 'Whatever. I don't like labels' is well-worn territory but works because of Aubrey Plaza's delivery and the character's established voice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A motel owner inviting us to his room? That's not a Red Flag, that's a Red Flag factory. That's where Red Flags are manufactured.

jokes.text: Leslie asks if her dress says 'Hello, general assembly, I've come to Indianapolis to accept your commendation' — and gets the answer 'As much as any one dress could'
jokes.setup: Leslie is obsessing over her outfit choice for the Statehouse ceremony
jokes.punchline: She phrases the requirement as an impossibly specific semiotic task; Ann's answer is technically accurate but diplomatically noncommittal
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie joke — her need for clothes to communicate exact institutional messages is pure character. Ann's response is a well-calibrated straight-woman line. The joke lands on the absurdity of the original question more than Ann's answer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So we're driving past this place called 'The Wax Museum of Broken Dreams,' and I'm like, 'Finally, a venue that understands my aesthetic.' Turns out it's just where they throw away the failed wax figures. Which, honestly, is even better. Do you know how they dispose of them? They have this whole system. They melt them down, but apparently some of the wax is mixed with human hair and teeth from the 1970s, so they can't just dump it anywhere. There's actually a specific landfill in Nevada that's designated exclusively for failed celebrity wax figure disposal. It's called the 'Hall of Shame Valley.' I want to be buried there.

jokes.text: Leslie's immediate 'What? That lying bastard.' before Ann has provided any evidence of cheating
jokes.setup: Ann says 'I think Chris is cheating on me'
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately, unconditionally sides with Ann and condemns Chris before a single fact is established
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie best-friend behavior — instantaneous unconditional loyalty before any evidence. 'That lying bastard' as a first response is funnier because of the speed and totality of the condemnation. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Leslie's immediate reversal: 'Oh, then I'm sure he's not cheating on you. And if he is, he's a monster. And if he's not, you guys are great together. But if he is, I will kill him.'
jokes.setup: Ann admits she has no actual proof of cheating
jokes.punchline: Leslie rapidly hedges and then re-condemns, ending on a murder threat, all with equal sincerity
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with a great escalating structure. Leslie tries to be rational, but each 'if he is' clause drags her back to full condemnation, ending with a genuine murder threat delivered calmly. The rhythm is perfect — it keeps building and the final 'I will kill him' lands hard because it's so matter-of-fact. Pure Leslie Knope best-friendship logic at its finest. Justifies the 8+ score: it has originality, perfect character integration, and the punchline earns its impact through structure rather than shock.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you need a doorbell. What if someone important needs to reach you?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If they're important, they'll know not to visit. I have a moat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You don't have a moat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: 'In high school, they used to call me Angela Lansbury. But that was because of my haircut.'
jokes.setup: Leslie brags she'll be able to detect if Chris is cheating because she was called 'Angela Lansbury' — implying sleuthing ability
jokes.punchline: It was because of her haircut, not her detective skills
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection. The setup makes you think she's going to brag about her investigative prowess à la Murder She Wrote. The punchline deflates this immediately with a self-deprecating detail she delivers without any embarrassment. The callback to Angela Lansbury specifically is original and well-chosen. The joke also retroactively makes you imagine young Leslie with an old-lady haircut, which is an additional visual bonus. Highly quotable and perfectly economical.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, why do you have seventeen identical cardigans in your closet?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, Leslie, I've found that a quality cardigan is a wardrobe staple. Each one is precisely the same thread count and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They still have the tags on them.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm very careful with my clothing investments.

jokes.text: 'Hey, champ.' / 'Hey, champ...ion.'
jokes.setup: Tom approaches Ben to invite him out, clearly doing it as a favor to Leslie
jokes.punchline: Tom starts with casual 'Hey, champ' then immediately over-corrects mid-word to 'champion' — revealing his attempt to seem friendly is effortful and slightly off
jokes.explanation: A small but precisely executed joke. The mid-word self-correction 'champ...ion' reveals Tom catching himself being dismissive and awkwardly overcorrecting. It's funny because the overcorrection makes it worse. Great economy — the whole joke is one interrupted word.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know Tom Haverford. Tell him Ben Wyatt sent you and you'll get a discount.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Tom Haverford? Never heard of him.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No, Tom... Haverford. He's very well-known.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: That's the fakest name I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Ben's alternative evening: the motel owner screening 'Hope Floats' in the lobby and inviting him to watch
jokes.setup: Tom tells Ben he should come out tonight, implying Ben has nothing going on
jokes.punchline: Ben's actual plan is to watch a 1998 Sandra Bullock film screened by a motel owner in the lobby — which Tom immediately identifies as a murder setup
jokes.explanation: Good joke with two layers: Ben's pathetic social situation and Tom's paranoid reading of it as a murder plot. 'Hope Floats' is a perfectly chosen specific film — sad, obscure enough to be believable, specific enough to be funny. 'I think she's gonna murder you' is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My whole life has been a lie. Everything I believed in, everything I stood for... gone. Closed. Just like that.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't know who I am anymore. That steakhouse was the only place that understood me. The only place that got it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They took away my sanctuary. My temple. My reason for living between the hours of six and nine PM.

jokes.text: 'I think she's gonna murder you.'
jokes.setup: Ben describes the motel owner's invitation to watch Hope Floats in the lobby
jokes.punchline: Tom's completely casual, unhesitating assessment that this is a murder situation
jokes.explanation: The button to Joke 22. Works on its own — the certainty and speed of 'she's gonna murder you' with no hedging is funny. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Genuine concern for the welfare of inanimate steaks

jokes.text: Leslie pitching Indiana's second largest rocking chair as a road trip stop
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are driving to Indianapolis and she suggests detours
jokes.punchline: Her first pitch is 'Indiana's second largest rocking chair' — not the largest, the second largest
jokes.explanation: The 'second largest' detail is key — it implies Leslie knows about and accepts the hierarchy of giant rocking chairs. A perfect Leslie roadside attraction enthusiasm joke. Ron's flat 'No' is the ideal one-word response.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what's crazy? All these fancy French perfume names. 'Eau de Toilette.' 'Chanel No. 5.' Meanwhile, the most exotic thing I could name a perfume is 'Essence of Eagleton.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not exotic, that's just the next town over.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly! To someone in France, it IS exotic. 'Ooh, what is this mysterious scent?' 'Oh, it's just called Eagleton, darling.'

jokes.text: Dame Gervin's Misshapen Celebrity Castle — where Madame Tussaud's sends its failed wax figures, and if you can identify who it is, you get to take it home
jokes.setup: Leslie, undeterred by Ron's 'No,' suggests a second detour
jokes.punchline: A museum that is essentially a dumping ground for botched celebrity wax figures, with a prize system for identification
jokes.explanation: Genuinely inventive absurdism. The concept of a secondary market for failed celebrity wax figures — failed enough that Tussaud's rejected them — is wonderfully specific and detailed. The prize-for-identification mechanic is the inspired detail that pushes it from good to excellent. Only Leslie would earnestly promote this as a desirable attraction. High originality score is justified.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm calling it 'Cologne Number Five.' It's got notes of ambition, a hint of desperation, and that fresh scent of a guy who's about to pitch you something whether you want to hear it or not.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, that's not how you sell cologne.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh really, Jerry? Because I just sprayed some on you and you're still talking to me, which means it's working.

jokes.text: 'What's wrong with you, grouchy pants? I've been fasting all day to save room for Mulligan's.'
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Ron 'grouchy pants' for refusing her detour suggestions
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he's been fasting all day — not as a health choice but as strategic preparation for maximum meat consumption
jokes.explanation: Ron fasting for meat rather than spiritual or health reasons is perfectly in character. The framing — strategic dietary preparation for a steakhouse — recontextualizes fasting as a fundamentally Ron Swanson activity.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How do you always get free drinks?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have a system. I go to a bar, I find the saddest guy there, and I tell him he looks like my dead dad. Then I cry a little, and he buys me drinks all night.

jokes.text: Ron's speech about flecks of meat remaining in his mustache for weeks after a Mulligan's meal — 'and I refuse to clean it because every now and then, a piece of meat will fall into my mouth'
jokes.setup: Ron tries to convey to Leslie the sacred significance of Mulligan's steakhouse
jokes.punchline: His explanation involves intentionally maintaining meat-contaminated facial hair as a long-term snacking system
jokes.explanation: An all-time Ron Swanson bit. The concept of using one's mustache as a long-term meat delivery system — intentionally not cleaning it so ambient meat morsels fall into the mouth — is disgusting, absurdist, and utterly specific to Ron. The detail that 'every now and then a piece of meat will fall into my mouth' is the peak: passive, patient, and delivered as wisdom. This approaches the anchor examples in quality. Character integration is essentially perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Creepy Guy
dialogue.line: Hi there, I'm Dirk Thunderbottom.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the worst name I've ever heard. Go away.

jokes.text: Leslie casually reveals Chris Traeger is joining them for dinner, triggering Ron's outrage
jokes.setup: Ron has been solemnly preparing for his sacred steakhouse pilgrimage
jokes.punchline: Leslie casually mentions Chris — a health-obsessed person — is joining them for a dinner at a legendary steakhouse, and Ron says 'Damn it, woman!'
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from contextual irony — inviting the most health-conscious character to the most indulgent dinner is the setup, and Ron's explosive but economical 'Damn it, woman!' is the punchline. Works well because we understand immediately why Ron is horrified.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I told the waiter I had a very rare condition where I could only eat appetizers. He felt so bad for me, he kept bringing them out for free all night.

jokes.text: Chris's house foyer 'sends a message to the world about who you are' / 'And the front door provides energy flow and opportunity. You cannot limit that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron arrive at Chris's immaculate, spa-like home
jokes.punchline: Chris delivers new-age wisdom about his foyer with complete sincerity — the entranceway is a philosophical statement about limitlessness
jokes.explanation: Solid Chris Traeger character joke — his relentless positivity applied to home decor philosophy. The specific claim that a front door 'limits energy flow' is a good absurdist detail. Consistent with his character but not his funniest moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ron, try some of this salad. It's got kale, quinoa, and a light vinaigrette.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Chris, I respect you, but I'm going to have to stop you right there. A salad is what food eats. I don't eat salad. I eat red meat and precious metals.

jokes.text: Ron doesn't have a front door and won't tell Leslie his address
jokes.setup: Chris talks about what front doors say about a person
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals Ron has no front door and won't tell anyone where he lives — Ron's only response is 'Why?'
jokes.explanation: Ron not having a front door is great character comedy — his extreme self-sufficiency and anti-government/anti-social tendencies logically extend to not wanting anyone to be able to find him. 'Why?' as his response to 'where do you live?' is perfect deadpan. The juxtaposition against Chris's front-door philosophy is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm like Yoda, man. I'm wise beyond my years.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yoda is 900 years old. You're 37.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, you know what I mean.

jokes.text: Leslie notices many men's coats in Chris's closet; Chris says 'I like coats.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is snooping for evidence of a secret woman; she opens the coat closet
jokes.punchline: There are a suspicious number of men's coats — but Chris's explanation is simply 'I like coats,' which is both innocent and slightly unsatisfying
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of Leslie finding 'suspicious' evidence that turns out to have innocent explanations. 'I like coats' is a perfectly flat non-explanation. Works as setup for the pattern that pays off later.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Feinstein
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'undercover'? I thought that's when cops dress up like regular people to catch criminals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's... yes, that's what undercover means.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Feinstein
dialogue.line: Then how am I supposed to do it with my cologne? Do I dress the cologne up like a regular person?

jokes.text: Leslie notices the toilet seat is up — reaction beat / dawning horror
jokes.setup: Leslie asks to use the bathroom, still investigating; she enters
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, the toilet seat's up.' — delivered as damning evidence of a male-free household breach (or confirmation of female presence)
jokes.explanation: Functional but thin. The toilet seat joke is a classic sitcom shorthand and the script uses it as one of Leslie's 'clues.' It works within the plot but is the weakest of the evidence-finding sequence. The joke type is somewhat clichéd.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Feinstein
dialogue.line: I don't work with amateurs. It's beneath me. I only collaborate with professionals who understand the candy business at my level.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Feinstein
dialogue.line: Wait, what was that idea you just said? That's genius. I'm stealing that.

jokes.text: Ben tells the bartender he knows Tom — 'Tom Hammen... Hammenstein... Haverford' — trying to get a free drink
jokes.setup: Ben tries to invoke Tom's name to get a free drink at the Snakehole
jokes.punchline: He can't remember Tom's last name and fumbles through multiple wrong answers before landing on the right one
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. Ben's social ineptitude is perfectly displayed — he's trying to namedrop someone he barely knows at a club he's never been to. The specific wrong names ('Hammenstein') are funny because they're plausible enough to be embarrassing. His 'like my best friend' oversell makes it worse.

jokes.text: Tom vouches for Ben by confirming he has money — Ben immediately says 'Yes.' then 'No.'
jokes.setup: The bouncer/bartender asks Tom if Ben has money to pay for drinks
jokes.punchline: Ben confidently says 'Yes' — then immediately, involuntarily corrects himself to 'No'
jokes.explanation: Simple and perfectly structured. 'Yes.' — pause — 'No.' is maximum economy. Ben's reflexive honesty undercutting his own social strategy is great character work. The monosyllabic structure makes it land cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was promised a steak dinner. A real steak. Thick cut. Aged properly.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, I made a quinoa and kale salad with a tahini drizzle. It's locally sourced and has only 120 calories per serving.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Chris, I don't know what most of those words mean, and I'm concerned about the ones I do.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's really good for you! Studies show—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to sit down. And drink a scotch. And reconsider our friendship.

jokes.text: Ron banging on the door of Charles Mulligan's, which is closed for a health code violation
jokes.setup: Ron has been fasting all day, building up to the sacred Mulligan's experience; they arrive to find it closed
jokes.punchline: Ron cannot accept this and physically attacks the door — Leslie has to physically restrain him ('Ron, stop it! Ron?')
jokes.explanation: The payoff to an episode-long buildup. Ron has been established as treating this meal as a sacred event — fasting, photographing steaks — and his response to the closure (physical assault on the door, requiring Leslie's restraint) is proportionate within his character. The laugh comes from the earned investment. 'They boarded her up like she was some common warehouse' adds a beautiful second beat.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Brandi Maxxxx, and I work here at the club.

jokes.text: 'They just boarded her up like she was some common warehouse.'
jokes.setup: Charles Mulligan's is closed and boarded up for a health code violation
jokes.punchline: Ron eulogizes the steakhouse using the language of a man mourning a fallen comrade — 'like she was some common warehouse'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Like she was some common warehouse' implies profound disrespect — the steakhouse deserved better. The word 'common' does a lot of work. This is Ron's grief expressed through indignation at the indignity of the situation. Perfectly economical, highly quotable, and completely character-specific. Justifies 8+ scoring.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? We're just like Robin Hood. We steal from the rich and give to the poor.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not what we're doing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, seriously. We're Robin Hood. I'm Robin Hood.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Robin Hood stole from corrupt tax collectors to return money to the people. You're taking free samples from Costco.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, but the principle is the same. I'm a hero.

jokes.text: 'What happened to the steaks that were in there when they closed? Do you think they got eaten?'
jokes.setup: Ron is devastated about Mulligan's being closed
jokes.punchline: His genuine concern is for the fate of the steaks — not the business, not the employees, the steaks — and he asks this with the gravity of someone asking about survivors of a disaster
jokes.explanation: Exceptional. Ron's moral universe is revealed: the only tragedy in Mulligan's closing is the fate of the steaks. 'Do you think they got eaten?' has the breathless hope of disaster relief — please tell me they survived. The follow-up pause where he genuinely hopes for a positive answer is implied and devastating. Character integration is as high as it gets.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, why do you have concealer in your medicine cabinet?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have pores, Ann. Large, cavernous pores. I'm not proud of it.

jokes.text: Tom listing Dennis Feinstein's scent names: 'Attack, yearning, thickening, itch, coma, sideboob'
jokes.setup: Tom is building up Dennis Feinstein's credentials as a master of fragrance
jokes.punchline: The scent names are increasingly bizarre and unsellable — 'thickening,' 'itch,' 'coma,' 'sideboob'
jokes.explanation: Brilliant list comedy. The scent names start evocative ('Attack,' 'yearning') then descend into the genuinely puzzling ('thickening'), the medical ('itch,' 'coma'), and the oddly specific ('sideboob'). The list has a perfect arc — each name worse than the last, and 'sideboob' as the closing entry is inspired. This is genuinely original absurdism, not just random weirdness — each name has an internal logic of someone trying to be edgy but failing in distinct ways.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris and I have a really healthy relationship. We communicate, we respect each other, we're building something real.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm moving to Washington, D.C. for a job at the National Park Service. I've already accepted.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? When were you going to tell me this?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I was going to tell you tonight. But also, I'm going to be seeing someone else there. We're not exclusive anymore.

jokes.text: Dennis Feinstein's real name is Dante Fiero — he changed it to Dennis Feinstein because 'that's way more exotic in Pawnee'
jokes.setup: Tom suggests Feinstein should change his name to something more exotic for the perfume world
jokes.punchline: He already has an exotic Italian name — but changed it to a plain Jewish one because Pawnee is so parochial that 'Feinstein' reads as exotic there
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical writing about small-town parochialism. 'Dante Fiero' is a legitimately exotic name in any real-world context, but in Pawnee 'Dennis Feinstein' is more exotic. The joke lands multiple satirical targets simultaneously: small-town insularity, name-based discrimination, and the absurdity of the perfume industry's self-mythology. Excellent structure and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Ann thinks Chris broke up with her, but Chris thinks they're still together because he was being positive about their relationship issues.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's the perfect storm of Ann's relationship inexperience and Chris's relentless optimism.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I kind of forgot that you need money when you have a girlfriend.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are figuring out what to do tonight and realize going out costs money
jokes.punchline: Andy genuinely forgot this as a concept — not that he's broke, but that relationships require expenditure
jokes.explanation: Great Andy Dwyer line. The joke isn't that he's broke — it's that the concept 'relationships cost money' is something he had to relearn from scratch. The word 'forgot' rather than 'realized' implies he once knew this and then simply stopped knowing it. Pure Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann is so oblivious to the world around her. Like, she didn't even notice that the entire office was decorated for her birthday party.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Which makes me question her medical competence. Like, how many times has she looked at someone and been like, 'Yeah, you're fine,' when they actually had like, a huge growth on their face?

jokes.text: Leslie's fake interrogation of Chris about female relatives: 'Do you have any sisters? / Any aunts? / Girl cousins? / A youthful grandmother, perhaps?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to investigate whether Chris is cheating, asking oblique questions about women in his life while pretending to have a normal dinner conversation
jokes.punchline: The questions escalate to increasingly implausible suspects ('a youthful grandmother, perhaps?') and Chris finally calls it out: 'Did you forget how to have a conversation?'
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe comedy sequence. Leslie's increasingly desperate interrogation disguised as dinner conversation escalates beautifully — 'a youthful grandmother, perhaps?' is the perfect absurd peak. The escalation structure is clean and the payoff from Chris calling it out is well-earned. The tag 'Did you forget how to have a conversation?' is concise and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, my cologne smells like failure and broken dreams, which is basically my signature scent at this point. I've been wearing it since my first failed business venture, and I'm not about to change now. It's who I am.

jokes.text: Ron, informed Chris might be cheating on Ann: 'Ask her to bring some garlic salt. I'm worried Chris doesn't have any.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ron she's figured out Chris is cheating on Ann and Ann is coming up to confront him
jokes.punchline: Ron's only concern is whether Ann should bring garlic salt for the grilling — he has absorbed the emotional crisis and filed it away while focusing on meat seasoning
jokes.explanation: One of the best Ron jokes in the episode. Ron's complete inability to engage with emotional drama, redirected entirely to the practical concerns of grilling, is perfectly in character. 'I'm worried Chris doesn't have any' treats garlic salt as the genuine crisis while Ann's romantic devastation registers zero. The economy is immaculate — two sentences that tell you everything about Ron. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I had big dreams, you know? I was going to be something special. I was going to soar like an eagle.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Eagles are just birds, Tom. They're not even that smart. I saw one fly into a window once.

jokes.text: April and Ben's free stuff competition at the Snakehole — pigs in a blanket, mints, eventually $38 and $180 in tips
jokes.setup: April discovers she can get free things at a sleazy club by being a woman; she and Ben turn it into a competition
jokes.punchline: Ben acquires pigs in a blanket by claiming a 'pork deficiency'; both accumulate increasingly absurd free items
jokes.explanation: A good sustained comic thread that develops naturally from Ben and April's characters — both are resourceful misfits. 'Pork deficiency' is the best individual gag within it. The escalation to significant cash tips is a good payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: My mom called me to tell me that my boyfriend broke up with me. She found out from Facebook before I did.

jokes.text: 'I got this from a waiter. I told him I had a pork deficiency.'
jokes.setup: Ben and April are competing to get the most free stuff; Ben produces pigs in a blanket
jokes.punchline: His method was claiming a medical condition called a 'pork deficiency' to a sympathetic waiter
jokes.explanation: 'Pork deficiency' is an excellent original joke — a medical-sounding term applied to a non-medical need, said to a credulous waiter who apparently accepted it. The specificity of choosing pigs in a blanket as the desired item adds to the absurdism. Highly quotable, creative, and a surprisingly strong joke from Ben in a scene that's mostly April's.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He broke up with me at a picnic. At a picnic!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's horrible. Who breaks up with someone at a picnic?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A monster. But that's not even the worst part. He showed up with another woman.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Who was she?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I have no idea. He never introduced us. He just sat there eating potato salad with her while I stood there like an idiot.

jokes.text: 'Since I am not a rabbit, no, I do not.' — Ron declining salad
jokes.setup: Chris offers Ron salad at the backyard grill dinner
jokes.punchline: Ron declines by taxonomically distinguishing himself from animals that eat vegetables
jokes.explanation: A classic Ron Swanson line. 'Since I am not a rabbit, no, I do not' is perfectly constructed — the formal setup ('since I am not a rabbit') before the flat refusal gives it a mock-judicial weight. The logic is Ron-internal: rabbits eat salad; he is not a rabbit; therefore no salad. Highly quotable, character-perfect. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Give me all the bacon and eggs you have.

dialogue.speaker: Server
dialogue.line: Do you want it on the side?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Bring me all the bacon and eggs you have. Wait, wait. I'm worried what you just heard was, bring me a lot of bacon and eggs. What I'm saying is, I want all the bacon and eggs you have. Do you understand?

jokes.text: Leslie's passive-aggressive threat to Chris: 'anyone who'd hurt her is someone I would murder probably'
jokes.setup: Leslie steers dinner conversation toward Ann, trying to get Chris to reveal the alleged affair
jokes.punchline: She describes Ann as her best friend and the consequence for hurting her as probable murder, delivered conversationally with the qualifier 'probably'
jokes.explanation: The word 'probably' is the joke — it softens the murder threat just enough to make it dinner-table appropriate while keeping its core sincerity. A callback to Leslie's earlier kill-threat, now deployed as veiled interrogation. Works well.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, Tom. I have a question: do you want to smell like dreams? Because that's what you're about to do to Dennis.

jokes.text: Tom approaches Dennis Feinstein: 'I'm the Yoda of networking' / Ben: 'Well, Yoda wouldn't actually need networking. His powers were more spiritual.'
jokes.setup: Tom declares himself 'the Yoda of networking' as he approaches Feinstein
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately and pedantically corrects the metaphor — Yoda's powers were spiritual, not social
jokes.explanation: Ben's nerd-pedantry is perfectly deployed here. The joke is that Tom is in his element trying to be smooth and cool, and Ben derails it by engaging earnestly with the Star Wars metaphor. 'Shut up, you nerd' as Tom's response is the ideal button. Strong character contrast.

jokes.text: Dennis Feinstein: someone just pitched him a cologne called 'Sluts' — 'I'm gonna tell you what I told him... although it's a great name and I'm probably gonna steal it.'
jokes.setup: Feinstein explains he gets pitched colognes all day and is about to dismiss Tom
jokes.punchline: He mentions a previous pitch for a cologne called 'Sluts,' sets up to reject it, then reverses to admit it's a great name he'll probably steal
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection. The setup implies Feinstein rejected 'Sluts' as a cologne name, which would be reasonable. The reversal — 'it's a great name and I'm probably gonna steal it' — reveals Feinstein's character: amoral, opportunistic, completely without shame. The 'probably' hedging is a funny detail. Feinstein is established as a great recurring villain in this exchange.

jokes.text: Feinstein's assessment of Tommy Fresh: 'It smells like somebody spilled Chinese food in a bird cage.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been hyping Tommy Fresh all episode; Feinstein finally smells it
jokes.punchline: The precise, evocative description of failure: 'Chinese food in a bird cage' — specific, awful, somehow you can smell it
jokes.explanation: Excellent original simile. 'Chinese food spilled in a bird cage' is specific, gross, and evocative in exactly the wrong ways for a cologne. The combination is disgusting: food smell + animal smell + the particular staleness of both. This is the payoff to the Tommy Fresh thread and it's a strong one. High quotability — this phrase sticks in the mind. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tom's confused response: 'As in, it's hilarious how awesome it is?'
jokes.setup: Feinstein says Tommy Fresh is 'a gag scent. Hilarious.'
jokes.punchline: Tom mishears the devastating insult as a compliment and tries to confirm it
jokes.explanation: Tom's desperate optimism converting a clear insult into a possible compliment is a good character moment. 'As in, it's hilarious how awesome it is?' is the specific phrasing of someone trying to will a good outcome into existence.

jokes.text: Ron sees portobello mushrooms on the grill: 'Where's the steak?' / Chris: 'There's no steak. That's a healthier option.' — Ron faints
jokes.setup: Ron is grilling at Chris's and expecting meat; he discovers portobello mushrooms instead
jokes.punchline: Ron apparently faints or has a near-collapse at the news that there is no steak — Leslie has to call for 'a cold compress'
jokes.explanation: The climax of the Ron-steak arc. After all the buildup — the fasting, the photographs, the mustache meat, the steakhouse door assault — Ron is taken out not by a bullet but by the news that Chris has served mushrooms. His physical collapse is the perfect punctuation to the whole storyline. Chris's earnest 'it's a healthier option' makes it worse. Character integration is as high as it goes — this could only happen to Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: April pretends to work as a waitress by claiming her dad owns the club ('I'm Janet Snakehole') to get free drinks for the table
jokes.setup: April and Ben are competing to get the most free stuff; April needs to escalate
jokes.punchline: April invents a persona ('Janet Snakehole,' daughter of the club owner) and orders a round on the house — it works
jokes.explanation: 'Janet Snakehole' works as a joke on its own (the name is perfect) and as character comedy — April's ease with manipulation and performance. The fact that it works instantly shows how completely she commits to the bit. The name 'Janet Snakehole' becomes a beloved running character for April across the series.

jokes.text: Mint/gum exchange — bartender is 'out of everything, sir'
jokes.setup: Ben asks for gum; no gum. Mints? No mints. Do you have anything? 'Out of everything, sir.'
jokes.punchline: The formally polite 'sir' attached to a complete absence of hospitality — delivered with total seriousness
jokes.explanation: A small but tight joke. 'Out of everything, sir' is the best iteration — the 'sir' is politely absurd when the answer is complete negation. Works as escalation within the gag.

jokes.text: April: 'We are like Robin Hood. We steal from the club and we give to ourselves.'
jokes.setup: April and Ben have been accumulating free items from the club
jokes.punchline: April reframes their petty larceny as Robin Hood, then immediately acknowledges the self-serving nature — 'we give to ourselves'
jokes.explanation: April undercuts the romantic Robin Hood framing in the same breath she invokes it. The twist ('we give to ourselves') is the key — it's a self-aware corruption of the myth that perfectly captures April's amoral but honest worldview.

jokes.text: Chris explains the pink razor: 'I shave my legs for swimming, and women's razors work better. Men's razor technology hasn't figured out how to properly contour the shinbone.'
jokes.setup: Ann has found a women's razor in Chris's shower and is convinced it's evidence of cheating
jokes.punchline: Chris calmly explains he shaves his legs for swimming performance and offers an informed critique of men's razor engineering
jokes.explanation: Excellent because the explanation is completely plausible and even reasonable — Chris Traeger, elite triathlete, would absolutely shave his legs and have opinions on razor contour technology. The specificity of 'the shinbone' elevates it. It's both character comedy and a deft subversion of Ann's paranoia.

jokes.text: Chris on the concealer in his medicine cabinet: 'I'm a human being. Sometimes I get blemishes. I'm not perfect.'
jokes.setup: Ann finds concealer, convinced it's more evidence; Chris responds
jokes.punchline: Chris Traeger — the most relentlessly positive, self-optimizing person on the show — conceding that he 'sometimes gets blemishes' and 'is not perfect' is played as a humbling admission
jokes.explanation: 'I'm not perfect' from Chris Traeger is funny precisely because he manifestly believes the opposite. The gravity with which he confesses to occasional blemishes — as if this is genuinely difficult to admit — is a perfect character joke.

jokes.text: The reveal: Chris broke up with Ann last week, but Ann didn't realize it
jokes.setup: Ann has come to Indianapolis to confront Chris about cheating
jokes.punchline: He wasn't cheating — he had already broken up with her, but she missed it entirely
jokes.explanation: The big structural reveal of the B-plot. The twist works because it reframes everything — all of Ann's 'evidence' of cheating was actually evidence of post-breakup distance she didn't register. It's also a good character joke about Chris being so gentle and positive that a breakup conversation got lost.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: Ann has never been dumped before, and Chris was so positive the breakup didn't register — 'it does kind of make you wonder how good of a nurse she is'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains how Ann missed the breakup conversation
jokes.punchline: She can't help adding the dig: if Ann is this bad at understanding what people are telling her, what does that mean for her patients?
jokes.explanation: An excellent Leslie confessional — she's being Ann's best friend while simultaneously, accidentally, delivering a devastating critique of Ann's professional competence. The 'although it does kind of make you wonder how good of a nurse she is' is a perfect throwaway that lands hard. Leslie's inability to fully suppress her honest assessments even when defending people she loves is a core comedic trait.

jokes.text: Ann realizes she kissed Chris after the breakup, met his parents, etc. — and Chris confirms all of this with increasing awkwardness
jokes.setup: Ann is reconstructing the timeline of her post-breakup behavior with dawning horror
jokes.punchline: Chris confirms each item — the kiss ('as enjoyable as that was, I did find it odd'), the parents ('I'm sure they're great people, but strange') — with polite bewilderment
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe escalation. Chris's responses are pitch-perfect — 'as enjoyable as that was, I did find it odd' is a masterpiece of diplomatic understatement, and 'I'm sure they're great people, but strange' for the parents-meeting is devastating. Each confirmation of Ann's post-breakup behavior makes the situation worse in a beautifully structured sequence.

jokes.text: Ben, dejected about Tommy Fresh, gets comforted by Tom who says: 'I can smell your dreams, Tom. And honestly, they smell ing terrible.'
jokes.setup: Tom is consoling Ben after Feinstein's rejection of Tommy Fresh; Tom begins sentimentally 'I can smell your dreams, Tom. I can.'
jokes.punchline: 'And honestly, they smell ing terrible.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with perfect setup and punchline structure. Tom builds up what sounds like a supportive, poetic declaration ('I can smell your dreams') — then subverts it completely with 'they smell ing terrible.' The comedy is in the swerve from apparent warmth to brutal honesty delivered in the same sincere voice. Highly quotable, great economy. The callback to the scent theme is elegant.

jokes.text: April wins the free stuff competition with $180 in tips
jokes.setup: Ben triumphantly shows $38 in tips; April responds
jokes.punchline: April produced $180 — nearly 5x as much — with no explanation of how
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the free stuff running gag. $180 with no explanation beats $38 decisively and the gap is funny. Works as a character statement about April's effortless social manipulation.

jokes.text: 'We should give it back.' — followed by: they keep the toilet paper
jokes.setup: April and Ben have accumulated significant cash and goods from the club
jokes.punchline: Momentary moral crisis — 'we should give it back' — followed by April keeping the toilet paper ('I feel bad, but I need it')
jokes.explanation: The moral code revealed: return the money, but toilet paper is a necessity. April's pragmatism about what constitutes an acceptable theft is a good character moment. 'I feel bad, but I need it' is a solid button.

jokes.text: Ann's bad breakup history montage: a guy's mom called to break up for him; broke her kneecap on a date and was abandoned; a guy got on one knee to beg her to never call again; a guy broke up in the shower; skywriting; the picnic where 'don't eat anything, Rebecca's coming'
jokes.setup: Leslie drives Ann home; Ann processes her embarrassment by listing her humiliating breakup history
jokes.punchline: Each breakup is worse than the last, escalating to 'don't eat anything, Rebecca's coming' — with the final tag 'Who was Rebecca?' / 'Yeah. Exactly.'
jokes.explanation: An exceptional list escalation sequence. Each breakup is more creative and humiliating than the last: the proxy mom call, the kneecap fracture abandonment, the inverse-proposal, the shower dumping, the skywriting (which could go either way — the ambiguity is funny), and finally the picnic revelation of Rebecca. 'Don't eat anything, Rebecca's coming' is the peak — the specificity of the food prohibition, the cheerful cruelty, and the mystery of Rebecca. 'Who was Rebecca?' / 'Yeah. Exactly.' is the perfect button — two words acknowledging the unanswerable nature of the wound. Strong structure, high originality in the individual scenarios.

jokes.text: 'This isn't a steak. Why would you call it that on your menu?' — Ron at a diner
jokes.setup: Ron and Chris end up at a 24-hour diner after the mushroom collapse; Ron ordered steak
jokes.punchline: What was called a steak on the menu does not meet Ron's standards for steak — and he demands an explanation for the false advertising
jokes.explanation: A continuation of the steak saga. Ron's outrage at the semantic violation — calling something a steak when it doesn't qualify — is character-perfect. The waiter's defeated 'I don't know what to tell you, man' is a good straight-man response.

jokes.text: 'Just give me all the bacon and eggs you have.' / 'Wait, wait — I worry what you just heard was Give me a lot of bacon and eggs. What I said was give me all the bacon and eggs you have.'
jokes.setup: Ron's steak was unsatisfactory; he pivots to an alternative order
jokes.punchline: He pre-emptively clarifies that 'all' means literally all — not a large portion, but the entire supply in the diner — and confirms this with grave seriousness
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best Ron Swanson moments in the series. The joke's genius is in its structure: Ron anticipates the waiter's misinterpretation and corrects it before it can happen, with the formal precision of a legal document — 'I worry what you just heard was...' The rhythm and repetition are perfect. 'All the bacon and eggs you have' as a legitimate order, confirmed twice with no irony, is the platonic ideal of Ron Swanson comedy. It approaches the 9.5 anchor in quality, is among the most quotable lines in Parks and Rec history, and has become a cultural touchstone. Fully justifies the top score in this episode.

jokes.text: Tom invents the 'tommytini': 'It's just vodka and a bunch of cinnamon.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben are drinking together after Feinstein's rejection
jokes.punchline: The tommytini sounds disgusting — vodka and 'a bunch of cinnamon' is not a cocktail, it's a dare
jokes.explanation: A minor Tom joke. Branding his own cocktail while wallowing in failure is consistent character behavior, and the drink description ('a bunch of cinnamon') is appropriately terrible. Modest laugh.

jokes.text: Tom's cocktail is called a 'tommytini' — just vodka and a bunch of cinnamon
jokes.setup: Ben is introduced to Tom's signature drink
jokes.punchline: 'It's just vodka and a bunch of cinnamon' — the complete simplicity behind the grandiose name
jokes.explanation: Tom would absolutely have a signature cocktail. The joke is the gap between the branding ('tommytini') and the reality (vodka + cinnamon). 'That sounds gross' from Ben validates the audience's reaction and the casual 'yeah' from Tom confirms he doesn't care.

jokes.text: Ben orders a Miller Lite — Tom: 'Everybody knows. That's your drink.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks for a Miller Lite
jokes.punchline: Tom already knew — implying Ben is the most predictable, middle-American, boring drinker imaginable, and that this is public knowledge
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody knows' is the key — it implies Ben's basic taste is so totemic that it precedes him. A quick, efficient character joke that contrasts Tom's cocktail culture with Ben's wholesome Midwestern defaults.

jokes.text: Everyone at the Snakehole knew Ann kissed Chris post-breakup — 'We were all seriously confused about that. Who's we? What are you...? Oh, God.'
jokes.setup: Tom casually mentions Ann tried to kiss Chris; Ann is mortified to learn it was public knowledge
jokes.punchline: 'We were all seriously confused about that' — revealing that Ann's post-breakup behavior was observed and discussed by multiple people
jokes.explanation: Ann's humiliation deepens: it wasn't a private misunderstanding but something 'we' were all 'seriously confused about.' Her 'Oh, God' as she processes 'we' being multiple people is a nice cringe beat. A good callback payoff.

jokes.text: April admits she kept the toilet paper from the club: 'Yes. I feel bad, but I need it.'
jokes.setup: After deciding to give back the money, April is asked if she returned everything
jokes.punchline: She kept the toilet paper because she needs it — a completely practical reason delivered with equal parts guilt and resolution
jokes.explanation: A nice coda joke. April's code of ethics has one practical exception: bathroom supplies. 'I feel bad, but I need it' is a perfect small moral compromise delivered with April's characteristic flat affect.

jokes.text: Tom sprays Dennis Feinstein with Tommy Fresh through his car window as revenge
jokes.setup: Tom spots Feinstein's car; Ben and April hand him the Tommy Fresh; he sprays Feinstein through the window
jokes.punchline: The reactions — 'Oh my God, it's unbelievable. Oh!' — confirm Tommy Fresh is as horrifying as described
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback closure to the Tommy Fresh arc. Tom gets petty revenge on Feinstein using the rejected cologne as a weapon. The visual of Feinstein being gassed through his own car window by his own scent words is a good physical comedy payoff. 'Is it that bad? Oh my God, it's unbelievable' confirms Tommy Fresh's awfulness while giving Tom a small victory.

tmdb_overview: Ron and Leslie take a road trip to the big city in order to visit Ron's favorite place which happens to be a steakhouse, but Leslie has alternative motives for the trip.
insight: Indianapolis trip spawns 45 jokes in 45 minutes—character-driven absurdism at peak density.
